To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the suite of VOC measurements at TF during ICARTT 04 showed a large range of total OH reactivity, 2) the impact of local anthropgenic hydrocarbon sources such LPG leakage and fossil fuel was evident at both TF and AI, and 3) net monoterpene emission fluxes at TF during ICARIT 04 were comparable to current nighttime emission inventory estimates
the total reactivity of VOCs was larger at a continental site than a coastal site and that the reactivity was dominated by isoperne and the monoterperns at the continental site

the 24 h mean OH reactivity at TF and AI were 4.15 and 2.58 s−1, respectively, that propane leakage from LPG tanks was the major anthropogenic source, and that monoterpene emissions were comparable to current inventory estimates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of local sources on VOC concentrations and reactivity in the New England region.
the chemical characterization of the atmosphere in the coastal region of New England.
understanding the chemical processes that control air quality, and in particular the role of biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOC) in the chemistry of the troposphere.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the VOC data from ICARTT 04 provide a good basis for future modeling studies of VOCs in the northeast.

the observed hydrocarbon fluxes and reactivities at TF and AI were consistent with the hypothesis that the New England coastal environment was impacted by a combination of anthropogenic and biogenic sources during the ICART campaign.
the observed VOC reactivity and fluxes were consistent with previous studies in the northeast and the observed VOC concentrations were dominated by local sources and regional transport.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ICARTT campaign provided an excellent snapshot of the chemical and physical processes that occur in the New England region and the impact they have on the atmosphere and the environment.
the total OH reactivity at the marine site was lower than at the continental site.
the VOC reactivity and fluxes measured at TF and AI were comparable to those measured at other sites in North America, and were dominated by isoprenoids.
The main takeaway from our work is that
VOC measurements at continental sites in the Northeastern US are dominated by anthropogenic and local biogenic sources, with the former being a significant source of hydrocarbons.
VOCs in the New Hampshire and Maine coastal region are strongly influenced by anthropogenic emissions, particularly LPG leakage.
the New England region, which is characterized by a large marine component, has significant anthropogenic hydrocarbon emissions from LPG leakage, fossil fuel evaporation, and biogenic emissions.
